summary: Alder buckthorn, also called glossy buckthorn, is a shrub that forms dense thickets whose shade wipes out native tree seedlings, saplings and wildflowers, and it can change which trees make up the forest canopy. In New York City it forms infestations of several acres, mostly under black locust trees, and it has been described as one of the most damaging non-native plants in Pelham Bay Park in the Bronx. Birds and mice eat its fruit, and the fruit can also float and be carried by water.
history: Alder buckthorn is native to Eurasia. It was grown as an ornamental plant, though demand for it today is near zero. It is now found in all northeastern states and provinces except Delaware and Virginia.

handling.text: It resprouts vigorously when cut back, and burning usually just leads to more resprouting. Its seeds can stay alive in the soil for at least three years. In New York City parks like Kissena, cutting, killing or removing plants without permission from NYC Parks is against park rules, so report it instead.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
